h1:
Ang Thong on a Budget
Temples · Markets · Cheap Eats
intro: Ang Thong gives you a lot back for the little you spend. Most temples charge no entry fee, a small bowl of boat noodles still starts in the double-digit baht range, and the main sights are under two hours' drive from Bangkok. Plan it well and a few hundred baht a day is enough to pay respects at the giant Buddha, wander an old market, and eat well from morning to night. We put this plan together for anyone who wants a fun trip while keeping costs down — both as a single day return and as a budget overnight — with real per-person costs so you know what to expect.
chips: 🪙 A few hundred baht a day

blocks.html: For budget travellers, the good thing about Ang Thong is that there is almost nothing expensive here. Big-name temples like Wat Muang and Wat Khun Inthapramun are free to enter, the old market sells snacks for a handful of baht, and hotels in town start in the low hundreds of baht. The biggest single cost is usually petrol or transport rather than the sights themselves. So this plan focuses on routing the drive in a loop without doubling back, eating where locals actually go, and choosing a cheap place to stay if you want to overnight.

We picked the eateries and spots from real reviews and local sources. Prices are rough ranges and may shift with the day and what you order, but overall it still works out as good value compared with other provinces.

blocks.text: What Ang Thong on a budget looks like

items: Entry fees — almost all the main temples are free. Just bring some cash for donations as you see fit and parking at a few spots.
Food — a small bowl of boat noodles starts around 15–25 THB, the old market has snacks for a handful of baht, and a filling main meal runs no more than 60–80 THB.
Accommodation (if you overnight) — hotels in town start in the low hundreds of baht, with most averaging around 500–900 THB a night. Split a room and it's even cheaper.
Getting there — driving is the best value if there are a few of you. Petrol for a Bangkok round trip is around 400–600 THB per car, which is light once you split it.
Total per person — a single day return runs around 300–500 THB; add a split room rate for an overnight and you're looking at roughly 800–1,300 THB.

blocks.title: The key to a cheap trip
blocks.html: The cost you can squeeze the most is transport. If four of you come in one car, splitting the petrol leaves it at just over a hundred baht each — far cheaper than vans and songthaews around the province, and you get to roam freely too.

blocks.text: One-day timeline — temples, market, cheap eats

blocks.html: If you've only got a day and want to keep costs down, this plan starts at the giant Buddha at Wat Muang in the morning, then loops into the old market for cheap eats, and finishes at the reclining Buddha before heading home — all in one continuous loop without backtracking.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Start at the giant Buddha, end at the reclining Buddha

items.activity: Leave Bangkok on the Asia Highway (Route 32)
items.note: Set off early before traffic builds. Pack snacks or water in the car so you don't have to pay over the odds at stops along the way.

items.activity: Reach Wat Muang in Wiset Chai Chan to see the giant Buddha, the largest Buddha image in Thailand
items.note: The image stands about 95 m tall. Free entry; bring cash for a donation as you wish. Early on, before the sun is harsh, the white image looks great shot against the sky.

items.activity: Walk the model heaven-and-hell scenes and the lotus-petal wall around the temple
items.note: There's plenty of detail, so it's an easy wander — no extra charge.

items.activity: Head to Sala Chao Rong Thong, the old riverside market, for a late breakfast
items.note: This century-old market blends Thai-Chinese architecture and has boat noodles, traditional sweets, and grilled meatballs — cheap snacks you can graze on for ages.

items.activity: Drive into Ang Thong town for cheap small-bowl boat noodles at a well-known shop
items.note: Small bowls start in the double-digit baht. Order several and you'll still be full for under a hundred.

items.activity: Go to Pho Thong district to pay respects at the reclining Buddha at Wat Khun Inthapramun
items.note: An open-air reclining Buddha about 50 m long, dating back to the Sukhothai era. Free entry.

items.activity: Stop at Wat Ton Son in town to pay respects to Somdet Phra Si Mueang Thong, by the Chao Phraya
items.note: It sits on the riverside in town, an easy stop before heading back. You can stroll along the water here.
You'll be home around 18:00, ahead of the heavy evening traffic.

blocks.html: The dish Ang Thong is known for and one you can easily afford on a tight budget is boat noodles — a rich, concentrated broth, with small bowls in the double-digit baht. Ordering several at a time is completely normal here. We picked the shops that locals and visitors mention often, drawn from real reviews.

items.name: Ruea Thong Boat Noodles (near the monument)
items.blurb: A big shop with lots of seating and a steady stream of customers, serving both tom yum and clear broth. The broth is well balanced and small bowls are cheap — a good late-morning stop on the way through. Order several and you're still within budget.
items.meta: Boat noodles · small bowls from about ฿15–20

items.name: Tiao Ruea Yutya (in front of Ang Thong Hospital)
items.blurb: A local favourite in Ang Thong. The broth is bold enough that you don't need to season it, with nam tok, tom yum, and clear-broth options. A standout side is the braised pork over rice stir-fried with kaffir lime leaves. Open roughly 08:30–17:00.
items.meta: Boat noodles · Pho Sa, Mueang district

items.name: Lom Choei Noodles (Sala Chao Rong Thong market)
items.blurb: A well-known shop in the old market with very cheap bowls — perfect to snack on while you wander. Order several alongside some traditional sweets and you're still full for a handful of baht.
items.meta: Noodles · inside Sala Chao Rong Thong market

items.name: Sane Ang Thong Boat Noodles
items.blurb: A local shop with tom yum, clear broth, and pad thai at reasonable prices — good for a quick meal before moving on to the next temple.

items.name: Por Prathip Boat Noodles
items.blurb: On the Ang Thong–Pa Mok road in Sala Daeng, right on the route to and from Pa Mok, so it's an easy stop. Friendly prices.
items.meta: Boat noodles · Ang Thong–Pa Mok Rd

items.name: Pa Saeng Wonton Noodles with Red Pork (Sala Chao Rong Thong market)
items.blurb: A single-table stall in the old market serving tasty wonton noodles with red pork that people queue for. Come early or avoid the peak to skip the long wait.
items.meta: Wonton noodles · inside Sala Chao Rong Thong market

blocks.title: Snacks in the old market
blocks.html: Sala Chao Rong Thong has plenty of traditional sweets for a handful of baht — khanom khi khwai, steamed sticky-rice parcels, and a well-known grilled-meatball stall. Buy a little to nibble as you walk; even a full day of grazing won't break the budget. It's the best-value eating of the whole trip.

blocks.text: Wander the old Sala Chao Rong Thong market

blocks.html: If you want a free outing with real atmosphere, Sala Chao Rong Thong market in Wiset Chai Chan delivers. It's an old riverside market over a century old, lining the Noi River, with old wooden buildings blending Thai-Chinese architecture. Walking through costs nothing — your only spend is on whatever food you want to try.

items.name: Wooden buildings on the Noi River
items.blurb: Old wooden shophouses and a Chinese shrine, with a vintage feel. Free to walk and photograph — great if you like old markets and local food.

items.name: Food and sweets zone
items.blurb: Traditional sweets, noodles, and grilled meatballs for a handful of baht — a long, cheap graze and the highlight for budget travellers.

blocks.title: When to visit the market
blocks.html: Old markets like this are busiest from morning to midday, and several food stalls sell out before the afternoon. If you're mainly coming to eat in the market, aim to arrive in the late morning before noon to find more of it open.

blocks.text: How to overnight on a budget

blocks.html: If you'd rather not tire yourself out with a one-day round trip, an overnight in Ang Thong town isn't pricey. Town has hotels from the low hundreds of baht up to riverside resorts, with most averaging around 500–900 THB a night. With a few of you splitting a room it's even cheaper per head, and you can add the Pa Mok craft villages to a relaxed second day without rushing.

items: Pick a hotel in town — low-hundreds-of-baht rates are cheaper than riverside resorts, and you're close to the noodle shops and market for cheap food.
Split a room with a group — a twin shared between two or three people comes to just a few hundred each, far cheaper than going solo.
Book ahead via an app — compare a few sites before booking; weekdays are usually cheaper than long weekends.
Avoid festival dates — rooms fill fast and prices climb over long weekends. Go on a weekday for better rates and fewer crowds.

blocks.text: Per-person budget for a cheap Ang Thong trip

blocks.html: The figures below are rough ranges for a group of 3–4 sharing one car. Adjust up or down with your group size and eating style, but overall it still works out cheap for what you get to see.

items: Round-trip petrol (split) — around 120–180 THB per person with 3–4 in the car.
Food for the day — 2–3 bowls of noodles, market snacks, and dinner, around 150–250 THB per person.
Donations + parking — as you see fit, around 40–100 THB per person.
Total for a one-day return — around 300–500 THB per person.
If you overnight one night — add a split room rate of around 200–350 THB per person, for roughly 800–1,300 THB total.

blocks.title: Where you can save even more
blocks.html: Keep water and snacks in the car to cut spending at the sights, eat in the market and at noodle shops rather than sit-down restaurants, and if there are a few of you, sharing one car and splitting a room are the two things that bring the budget down most.

blocks.text: Getting there and planning a good-value trip

items: Drive yourself — the best value with a group. Take Route 32 (the Asia Highway) from Bangkok, about 100 km. The main temples and town have large car parks.

Van/coach — services run from Mo Chit to town and are cheap if you're solo, but within the province you'll need songthaews or to charter a vehicle, which isn't convenient for hopping between districts.
Route it without backtracking — start on the Wiset Chai Chan side (Wat Muang, Sala Chao Rong Thong market), then loop into town and Pho Thong to save petrol and time.
Pair it with Sing Buri or Ayutthaya — Ang Thong borders both, so with extra time you can extend the trip with almost no added transport cost.

faq.q: How much does a day trip to Ang Thong cost?
faq.a: For a one-day return with a few of you splitting the petrol, budget around 300–500 THB per person — covering your share of fuel, food for the day, and donations. Since the main temples like Wat Muang and Wat Khun Inthapramun are free, most of your spending goes on food and transport.

faq.q: How much is a bowl of Ang Thong boat noodles?
faq.a: Small bowls at the well-known shops mostly start around 15–25 THB, and ordering enough to fill up usually comes to no more than 60–80 THB per person. In Sala Chao Rong Thong market there are stalls cheaper still — great for keeping costs down.

faq.q: Is Sala Chao Rong Thong market free, and what's there to eat?
faq.a: Walking through the market is free. It's a riverside market over a century old on the Noi River, with old wooden buildings and a Chinese shrine. There's plenty of food for a handful of baht — noodles, wonton noodles, traditional sweets, and grilled meatballs. It's the best-value eating for budget travellers.

faq.q: Where can I stay cheaply overnight in Ang Thong, and how much is it?
faq.a: Ang Thong town has hotels starting in the low hundreds of baht, with most averaging around 500–900 THB a night. With a few of you splitting a room it comes to just a few hundred each. We'd suggest a hotel in town, since it's cheaper than a riverside resort and close to the noodle shops and market.

faq.q: Is there an entry fee for temples in Ang Thong?
faq.a: The main temples — Wat Muang, Wat Khun Inthapramun, and Wat Ton Son — are free to enter. Just bring cash for donations as you wish and parking at a few spots. That makes them ideal for a budget trip.
